x_to_y: This edge encodes the causal effect of \(x\) on \(y\): changing \(x\) is assumed to directly change \(y\), holding other relevant factors fixed. The main threats are omitted confounders that affect both \(x\) and \(y\), reverse causality if \(y\) also feeds back into \(x\), or measurement error in \(x\) that attenuates the estimated effect. Next, the researcher should justify the identifying variation in \(x\) (e.g., experimental assignment, a credible instrument, or a quasi-experimental design), and probe robustness by checking balance/placebo tests and sensitivity to adding plausible controls or alternative specifications.
y_to_z: Economically, the edge \(y \rightarrow z\) encodes that changes in \(y\) cause changes in \(z\), meaning \(y\) is a direct determinant of the outcome/process measured by \(z\). The main risks to a valid causal estimate are omitted confounders that affect both \(y\) and \(z\), reverse causality if \(z\) also feeds back into \(y\), and post-treatment conditioning if you control for variables influenced by \(y\). Next, the researcher should map and justify the adjustment set implied by the DAG (identify plausible common causes of \(y\) and \(z\)), check timing/ordering to rule out simultaneity, and run robustness/sensitivity checks (e.g., alternative controls, placebo outcomes/exposures) consistent with the proposed causal pathway.
